title: Draws, and never resigning
blurb: Not every game is won or lost. Learn the ways a game ends in a draw, how to save a lost position, and why you never resign.
deeperTitle: Week 1 review quiz and puzzle set

core.title: A draw is a result too
body: A game can end in a **draw**, half a point each. The main ways: **stalemate**, the **same position three times**, **not enough pieces to checkmate**, or both players **agree**.
When you are losing, a draw is a great result. This lesson is about getting one.

board.caption: Stalemate: Black has no legal move and is not in check.

core.prompt: White has a king and a bishop. Black has only a king. How does this game end?
options: A draw: nobody can ever give checkmate
White wins by chasing the king
core.explain: A king and a bishop (or a king and a knight) cannot checkmate a lone king, so the game is drawn on the spot. King against king is a draw too.

core.prompt: Now White has a king and a rook against a lone king. What happens with good play?
options: It is a draw, just like the bishop
core.explain: A king and a rook can force checkmate (you met the ladder and the king-and-rook mate on Day 4). A lone bishop or knight cannot. When you are losing, trading down to that is one way out.

core.title: The same position three times
body: If the **same position** appears **three times**, a player can claim a draw. So can they after fifty moves with no capture and no pawn move.
The classic way to force it is **perpetual check**: keep giving check, and their king has to keep stepping to the same squares.

board.caption: White is behind in material, but Black’s king has nowhere to hide.

core.prompt: White is losing on points. Find the check that forces a draw by perpetual check.
core.hint: Check the king from g6. Where can it go? Then check again so that it has to come back.
core.explain: **Qg6+** forces **Kh8**, then **Qh6+** forces **Kg8**, and **Qg6+** again. The knight on e6 covers f8 and g7, and nothing can block or capture, so Black cannot escape. The position repeats: a draw.

core.title: Stalemate can save you
body: Stalemate is not only something to avoid. When **you** are losing, it can save you: have no legal move while you are **not in check**.
The trick is to give up your last mobile piece, so that your opponent has to take it.

board.caption: Black is a queen and a bishop down. Black’s king is boxed in by the queen.

core.prompt: You are Black, far behind. Find the move that saves the game.
core.hint: Your king cannot move. Give up your rook with check, so that White has to take it.
core.explain: **Re1+** is check. White’s king cannot move and the queen cannot block, so the only legal reply is **Bxe1**. Now Black has no legal move and is not in check: **stalemate**, a draw.

core.prompt: Now the other side. You are winning. Checkmate in one. One tempting queen move would be stalemate, so check each square.
core.hint: The queen must give check, not just trap the king.
core.explain: **Qg7#**, **Qg8#**, **Qh1#** and **Qh2#** all mate. **Qg6** looks strong, but it is stalemate: the king has no move and is not in check.

core.title: Never resign
body: Resigning gives away the half point you might still get. Strong players resign rarely, and beginners should almost never.
Opponents miss checks, miss stalemate tricks and run out of time. Make them find the win.

core.prompt: You are a queen down against someone who plays fast. What is the best plan?
options: Play on, set traps and look for checks and stalemate
Offer a draw on every move
core.explain: Fast players blunder. Keep making threats, give checks when they are safe, and watch for a perpetual or a stalemate. You lose nothing by trying.

core.prompt: You are clearly winning, and your opponent offers a draw. What should you do?
options: Decline and keep playing for the win
core.explain: A draw is only half a point. When you are winning, play on, and watch out for stalemate. When you are the one losing, a draw offer is worth taking.

core.title: Escape artists
core.intro: You are losing in every one of these, and you have a way out. Find the perpetual check or the stalemate trap.

puzzles.hint: You are Black. Check the king from g3, and keep checking.
puzzles.explain: The knight on e3 covers f1 and g2, so the king can only shuffle between g1 and h1. **Qg3+**, **Qh3+**, **Qg3+**: a perpetual check.

puzzles.hint: Black’s king is boxed in by its own pieces. Check on the g-file.
puzzles.explain: **Qg5+** forces the queen to block on g7. **Qd8+** forces it back to f8, and **Qg5+** starts again. Black cannot break the cycle.

puzzles.hint: Your king is boxed in by the queen. Give up your rook with check.
puzzles.explain: **Re8+** can only be answered by **Bxe8**, and then White has no legal move and is not in check: stalemate.

puzzles.hint: You are Black. Your king is boxed in. Give up the rook with check.
puzzles.explain: **Rb1+** can only be answered by **Rxb1**, because the queen on b6 is blocked by the rook on b3. Then Black has no legal move and is not in check: stalemate.

deeper.title: Week 1 in a minute
body: Six days, six ideas: how games end, the opening rules, how pieces see, the must-know mates, forks, and the checklist.
Here is one or two questions from each. Answer first time and your score counts.

deeper.prompt: Day 1. Checkmate in one. Your king is helping.
deeper.hint: Put the queen on a square next to the black king that your own king also guards.
deeper.explain: **Qg7#**. The queen attacks the king, your king protects her, and no square is left to run to.

deeper.prompt: Day 1. Which of these ends the game with a win for you?
deeper.explain: Winning the queen or giving check does not end the game. Only checkmate, resignation, time or abandonment do.

deeper.prompt: Day 2. Which opening start follows all three ideas?
deeper.explain: A centre pawn, then a knight, then a bishop. Next would come castling. The other two waste moves on the edge or bring the queen out too soon.

deeper.prompt: Day 3. White to move. Tap the black piece that nobody defends.
deeper.explain: The d7 pawn guards the knight, the bishop guards the d7 pawn, and the king guards the other pawns. But **nobody guards the bishop on f5**, so the queen can simply take it.

deeper.prompt: Day 3. Their bishop attacks your knight, and nothing protects it. Answer by **capturing** the attacker.
deeper.hint: Which of your pieces can take the bishop on g4?
deeper.explain: **hxg4**. The pawn takes the bishop and nothing takes back. Pawns are excellent at removing attackers.

deeper.prompt: Day 4. Checkmate in one. One tempting queen move would be stalemate, so check each square.
deeper.hint: The queen must give check, not just trap the king.
deeper.explain: **Qg7#**, **Qg8#**, **Qh1#** and **Qh2#** all mate. **Qg6** looks strong, but it is stalemate: the king has no move and is not in check.

deeper.prompt: Day 5. Fork the king and the queen with your knight.
deeper.hint: Find the square from which the knight attacks both the king and the queen.
deeper.explain: **Nf6+** attacks the king and the queen at once. The king must move, and then **Nxd7** wins the queen.

deeper.prompt: Day 6. White to move. Find the check that leads to checkmate in two.
deeper.hint: You have several checks. Which one leaves Black only one legal reply?
deeper.explain: **Qc8+** leaves Black one reply: the bishop must block on d8, because the king has no square. Then **Qxd8#** is checkmate. None of your other checks forces mate. Your queen is attacked by the bishop on e5, but with a check every move Black never gets to take it.

deeper.prompt: Day 6. Several pieces can be taken here, but only one capture wins material. Find it.
deeper.hint: Before you take anything, ask: is it protected? One black piece is not.
deeper.explain: **dxe5** wins a knight that nothing protects, and the pawn now attacks the knight on f6 as well. **Bxh7+** looks tempting, but the knight on f6 simply takes the bishop.

deeper.title: Week 1 puzzles
deeper.intro: One from each part of the week. Take your time.

puzzles.hint: Your king already covers the squares in front of the black king.
puzzles.explain: The king on b6 guards a7 and b7, so the rook only has to check along the back rank.

puzzles.hint: Look for the piece with no defender.
puzzles.explain: The knight on d5 had no defender, so the rook wins it for free.

puzzles.hint: Check from far away, so the king cannot take the rook.
puzzles.explain: The rook on h7 guards the 7th rank. Rc8 checks along the 8th, and the king cannot reach it.

puzzles.hint: You are Black. Jump to the square that checks the king and attacks the queen.
puzzles.explain: The knight on f3 attacks the king and the queen. After the king moves, the queen falls.

puzzles.hint: A queen check on the back rank. Where can Black block?
puzzles.explain: **Qa8+** forces the bishop to block on e8, and **Qxe8#** takes it with checkmate.

puzzles.hint: No check is needed. Aim at the weak pawn next to the king.
puzzles.explain: **Qg4** threatens **Qxg2#**, and the g2 pawn is pinned to the king, so White cannot take the bishop on h3 with it. The mate cannot be stopped.
